data_section_full_text:
In our primary sample, we study restatements of previously issued financial statements
where the first disclosure that the company may ⁄ will restate its financial statements
occurred during 2000 or 2001 and involved correction of non-GAAP reporting on Form
10-Ks originally issued for 1999 or 2000 or Form 10-Qs originally issued for 2000 or 2001.
We include restatements of 10-Qs because timely reviews of quarterly results were required
during our sample period, so quarterly financial statements clearly fall within the purview
of the audit committee.

We identified 157 firms announcing such restatements by searching the LEXIS-NEXIS
News Library and Form 8-K file. Restatements were identified using keyword searches
such as ‘‘restat’’, ‘‘revis’’, ‘‘adjust’’, and ‘‘error’’. Following similar restatement studies by
Abbott et al. 2004 and Agrawal and Chadha 2005, we selected a matched sample of
nonrestating firms. We matched on stock exchange, industry, and size. We measured firm
size in the year preceding the restatement using the market value of equity, and matched
within plus or minus 30 percent. <sup>13</sup> We also verified that control firms were not involved in

13. We match on stock exchange because of differences among exchanges in requirements related to audit
committee composition and audit committee financial expertise during our sample period. Based on the
conclusions of Bhojraj, Lee, and Oler 2003, we use the Global Industry Classifications Standard (GICS)
system to measure industry classification. Seventy-seven of the restatement firms were matched at the
eight-digit GICS code level, 14 firms were matched at the six-digit GICS code level, eight firms were
matched at the four-digit GICS code level, and five firms were matched at the two-digit level. There was
not a significant difference between the mean market value of equity for the restatement and nonrestatement groups (p-value    - 0.10), indicating that our size-matching procedure was effective.
